title: What Are Design Patterns?
summary: What a design pattern is (a named, reusable solution to a recurring design problem) and what it isn't, where the idea came from, the three Gang of Four categories, a quick UML primer, the two guiding principles, and an honest look at when a pattern helps versus when it's just over-engineering.

title: The SOLID Principles
summary: The five SOLID principles of object-oriented design — Single Responsibility, Open/Closed, Liskov Substitution, Interface Segregation, and Dependency Inversion — each with a tiny TypeScript example, plus how Dependency Inversion differs from Dependency Injection and Inversion of Control.

title: Factory Method
summary: The Factory Method pattern — define a method for creating an object but let subclasses decide which concrete class to instantiate, so the code that uses a product is decoupled from the code that creates it.

title: Abstract Factory
summary: The Abstract Factory pattern — provide an interface for creating whole families of related objects without naming their concrete classes, so an entire set of products can be swapped consistently, and how it differs from Factory Method.

title: Builder
summary: The Builder pattern — separate the step-by-step construction of a complex object from its final representation, avoiding unreadable 'telescoping' constructors, with a look at the popular fluent-builder variation in TypeScript.

title: Prototype
summary: The Prototype pattern — create new objects by cloning an existing 'prototype' instead of building them from scratch, with the crucial shallow-versus-deep-copy distinction and how it relates to (but differs from) JavaScript's own prototypal inheritance.

title: Singleton
summary: The Singleton pattern — ensure a class has just one instance with a global access point — presented honestly: how to build one, why many consider it an anti-pattern (global state, hidden dependencies, hard testing), and why in TypeScript a module is often the simpler single instance.

title: Adapter
summary: The Adapter pattern — wrap an object with an incompatible interface so it fits the interface your code expects, letting classes that couldn't otherwise cooperate (like third-party or legacy code) work together.

title: Bridge
summary: The Bridge pattern — split an abstraction from its implementation so the two can vary independently through composition, avoiding the combinatorial explosion of subclasses you'd get by combining every variant with inheritance.

title: Composite
summary: The Composite pattern — arrange objects into tree structures representing part-whole hierarchies, and give leaves and containers a shared interface so client code can treat a single object and a whole group of objects exactly the same way.

title: Decorator
summary: The Decorator pattern — wrap an object to add responsibilities dynamically while keeping the same interface, a flexible alternative to subclassing that lets you stack behaviors, and how it differs from the TypeScript language feature that shares its name.

title: Facade
summary: The Facade pattern — put a simple, unified interface in front of a complicated subsystem so clients can do the common thing with one easy call, without hiding the subsystem for those who need its full power.

title: Flyweight
summary: The Flyweight pattern — support very large numbers of objects by sharing the parts they have in common (intrinsic state) and keeping only the parts that differ (extrinsic state) outside, the one GoF pattern whose explicit purpose is saving memory.

title: Proxy
summary: The Proxy pattern — stand in for another object with the same interface to control access to it (lazy loading, permissions, caching, remote calls) — plus a side-by-side comparison of the four 'wrapper' patterns: Adapter, Facade, Decorator, and Proxy.

title: Chain of Responsibility
summary: The Chain of Responsibility pattern — pass a request along a chain of handlers so each one either handles it or forwards it to the next, decoupling the sender from whichever receiver ends up dealing with it.

title: Command
summary: The Command pattern — turn a request into a standalone object carrying everything needed to perform it, so requests can be passed around, queued, logged, and — crucially — undone, decoupling the object that triggers an action from the one that performs it.

title: Iterator
summary: The Iterator pattern — access the elements of a collection one by one without exposing how the collection stores them — and how TypeScript and JavaScript build it right into the language through Symbol.iterator, the iterator protocol, and generators.

title: Mediator
summary: The Mediator pattern — route communication between many objects through a single mediator instead of letting them reference each other directly, cutting a tangle of many-to-many links down to simple spokes around one hub.

title: Memento
summary: The Memento pattern — capture an object's internal state into an opaque snapshot that can be stored and later used to restore the object, all without exposing or breaking the object's encapsulation, the foundation of reliable undo.

title: Observer
summary: The Observer pattern — define a one-to-many dependency so that when a subject changes, all its registered observers are notified automatically — the idea behind event listeners, pub/sub, and reactive programming, taught with its real pitfalls like memory leaks from forgotten unsubscribes.

title: Strategy & State
summary: Two behavioral patterns with nearly identical structure but different intent — Strategy makes a family of algorithms interchangeable so a client can pick one, while State lets an object change its behavior (and often trigger its own transitions) as its internal state changes — taught together so you never confuse them.

title: Template Method
summary: The Template Method pattern — put the fixed skeleton of an algorithm in a base-class method and let subclasses fill in specific steps, keeping the overall structure constant while varying the details, and how it contrasts with Strategy's composition-based approach.

title: Interpreter & Visitor
summary: Two advanced behavioral patterns that work over object structures — Interpreter represents a small language's grammar as a tree of classes that evaluate themselves, while Visitor lets you add new operations to a structure of objects without modifying their classes, at the cost of making new element types harder to add.

title: Choosing Patterns & Avoiding Anti-Patterns
summary: The capstone — how to choose the right pattern (or none), why over-engineering and the 'Golden Hammer' are real dangers, how to refactor toward patterns instead of starting with them, the common anti-patterns to avoid, and a note that MVC, Dependency Injection, and Repository live beyond the Gang of Four.
